messages.author: e19ea506112fd25b
messages.subject: prediction with mixtures
parts:
Hi,

Is it possible to make predictions using mixture model?  Assuming normal mixture model below
what would be the generated quantities block to calculate predictive posterior? What would be the meaning of 95% credible interval of this predictive posterior?

Thank you,
Linas

data {
  int<lower=1> K; // number of mixture components
  int<lower=1> N; // number of data points
  real y[N]; // observations
}
parameters {
  simplex[K] theta; // mixing proportions
  real mu[K]; // locations of mixture components
  real<lower=0> sigma[K]; // scales of mixture components
}
model {
  real ps[K]; // temp for log component densities
  sigma ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
  mu ~ normal(0,10);
  for (n in 1:N) {
    for (k in 1:K) {
      ps[k] <- log(theta[k]) + normal_log(y[n],mu[k],sigma[k]);
    }
    increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(ps));
  }
}

messages.author: 3f22b207863d2049
messages.subject: Re: prediction with mixtures
parts:
In the generated quantities block, for each new data point that you want to predict:
  1. Draw mixture component index k from a categorical distribution with parameters theta.
  2. Draw random value from the k-th mixture component N(mu[k],sigma[k]).

Regarding the 95%-BCI: i.m.h.o. it is what it is; it's just not a very useful summary of a multimodal distribution.

messages.author: 3f22b207863d2049
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: prediction with mixtures
parts: Looks about right what your doing. It's just that you are using mixture component index k for all of the i random flow_pred values. Although this doesn't matter for the marginal distributions of each elements in flow_pred, it will matter for the distribution of combinations of the elements of flow_pred (sums, differences, products, average, etc.). If you want to fix this, just make sure to redraw k for each i-th element of flow_pred.

parts:
Whuuuu?  A parameter of 1e9???  I suggest you rescale the problem in something closer to natural units (for example, if your counts are in the millions, rescale using an offset multiplier of 1 million.  In general in statistical computing (not just Stan) it’s a good idea for parameters to have order of magnitude 1, not 1e9 or 1e-9.  People aren’t always aware of this because classical linear regressions and glms are scale-free.  But once you have priors, scale matters.  Also straight computational issues.

messages.author: e19ea506112fd25b
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] prediction with mixtures
parts:
Interestingly enough with increasing number of mixture components waic increased while Bayesian p-value of chi square test (http://www.bayesian-inference.com/posteriorpredictivechecks) decreased.  How to explain this?  The trace of some of the parameters of the model and model itself are attached.  Any input is welcome.  The R code to determine p-value is below.
goodness.of.fit.pearson <- function (y, y.new, mu)
{
#
# Goodness-of-Fit assessment in Bayesian analyses
#
Presidual <- array (NA, dim = c (nrow (y.new), ncol (y.new)))
fit <- rep (NA, nrow (y.new))
fit.new <- rep (NA, nrow (y.new))
for (i in 1 : nrow (y.new)) {
Presidual [i, ] <- (y - mu [i, ]) / sqrt (mu [i, ])
fit [i] <- sum (Presidual [i, ] ^ 2)
fit.new [i] <- sum (((y.new [i, ] - mu [i, ]) / sqrt (mu [i, ])) ^ 2)
}
mean.Presidual <- rep (NA, length (y))
for (j in 1 : length (y)) {
mean.Presidual [j] <- mean (Presidual [, j])
}
par (mfrow = c (1, 2))
plot (mean.Presidual, main = "Chi Square",
las = 1, xlab = "Index", ylab = "Mean of Chi Square")
abline (h = 0, lwd = 2, col = "red")
#
# Posterior predictive check
#
lim <- range (log (fit), log (fit.new))
plot (log (fit), log (fit.new),
main = paste ("Graphical posterior predictive check\n",
"chi square test", sep = ""),
las = 1, xlab = "Chi square for actual data set",
ylab = "Chi square for predicted data set", xlim = lim,
ylim = lim, cex.axis = 0.6)
abline (0, 1, lwd = 2, col = "red")
#
# calculate Bayesian p-value
#
mean (fit.new > fit) #Bayesian p-value
}

Thank you,
Linas

messages.author: 3f22b207863d2049
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: prediction with mixtures
parts: Why not just use rmultinom? which(rmultinom(1, 1, c(0.5,0.25,0.25)) == 1) will generate an index K from (1,2,3) with the listed probabilities.

On Friday, 1 May 2015 21:46:53 UTC+2, Linas Mockus wrote:
I found the code in R for categorical_rng
M <- 10000
P <- rep (1 / K, K)
c <- cumsum (P)
h <- histc (runif (M), c (0, c))

h$bin are M samples from categorical distribution

My question now is how to compare models - one model is a mixture of two negative binomials, another model is a mixture of three negative binomials.  Is waic a good measure?

Thank you,
Linas
On Fri, 01 May 2015 03:31:00 -0400, Luc Coffeng <lucco...@gmail.com> wrote:

In the generated quantities block, for each new data point that you want to predict:
  1. Draw mixture component index k from a categorical distribution with parameters theta.
  2. Draw random value from the k-th mixture component N(mu[k],sigma[k]).

Regarding the 95%-BCI: i.m.h.o. it is what it is; it's just not a very useful summary of a multimodal distribution.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] "one chain always breaks during warmup (before it reaches 10%) because poisson_rng rate parameter is > than 1e+9"
parts: Scale by adding an constant offset to your linear predictor. To follow Andrews example of scaling by a million: add ln(1e6) to eta as you feed it into neg_binomial_2_log. For problems with large numbers, this should improve computational efficiency. I don't think it will help prevent the sum of ln(1e6) and eta from reaching 1e9, but at least the values of the model parameters underlying linear predictor eta won't be so ridiculously large.

On Saturday, 2 May 2015 02:20:13 UTC+2, Linas Mockus wrote:
Counts include zeros and small numbers.  I have no clue how to scale it.  Would you please advice?

Thank you,
Linas
On Fri, 01 May 2015 17:24:13 -0400, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

Whuuuu?  A parameter of 1e9???  I suggest you rescale the problem in something closer to natural units (for example, if your counts are in the millions, rescale using an offset multiplier of 1 million.  In general in statistical computing (not just Stan) it’s a good idea for parameters to have order of magnitude 1, not 1e9 or 1e-9.  People aren’t always aware of this because classical linear regressions and glms are scale-free.  But once you have priors, scale matters.  Also straight computational issues.
A

On May 1, 2015, at 2:02 PM, Linas Mockus <linasm...@gmail.com> wrote:

Luc,

Thanks a lot.  The corrected code is attached.

Do you have any advice on the neg_binomial_rng?  I run two chains so one chain always breaks during warmup (before it reaches 10%) because poisson_rng rate parameter is > than 1e+9.  I put fmin but this doesn't help.  Can I implement categorical_rng in R? 

Thank you,
Linas
On Fri, 01 May 2015 11:47:21 -0400, Luc Coffeng <lucco...@gmail.com> wrote:

Looks about right what your doing. It's just that you are using mixture component index k for all of the i random flow_pred values. Although this doesn't matter for the marginal distributions of each elements in flow_pred, it will matter for the distribution of combinations of the elements of flow_pred (sums, differences, products, average, etc.). If you want to fix this, just make sure to redraw k for each i-th element of flow_pred.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] "one chain always breaks during warmup (before it reaches 10%) because poisson_rng rate parameter is > than 1e+9"
parts:
> On May 1, 2015, at 7:10 PM, Linas Mockus <linasm...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> It is somewhat confusing. Without generated quantities block it converges nicely. Mean is 2. The maximum of draws is also in the similar range: 30. However when I add generated quantities block with neg_binomial_2_log_rng it starts reporting that poisson_rng rate parameter is above 1e+9.

The very deep problem here is that Stan is using int arithmetic
and 1e9 is too large to sample reliably in the headroom of
an int.
> I assume neg_binomial is implemented as poisson-gamma mixture.

No, it's just coded directly as a density. The
latent parameter's marginalized out analytically.

> And this occurs very yealy (<10% in warmup). My solution to this is to replace generated quantities block with corresponding R code. However, I am using generated quantities for other problems - only neg_binomial has issues. I would love to use genera
> ted quantities always since it is more transparent.

I agree --- the real solution here is for us to move
everything to 64-bit computation on the inside of Stan.
That's something we need to do longer-term anyway, but
it's probably not going to happen any time soon.

- Bob
